input.question: Why is this year's flu vaccine so bad?
input.ground_truth: The flu vaccine is ordered based on the strains of flu circulating in the world approximately 6 months in advance of the US flu season to allow time to make the vaccine, distribute it, and administer it. In the time between the moment that the target flu strains were selected for inclusion into the vaccine and now the virus strains mutated and are now different from what is in the vaccine. This is not the first time it has happened and so long as the production cycle is 4-6 months it will continue to happen.

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why is this year's flu vaccine so bad?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you and your friends are playing a game where you try to guess what toy is hidden in a box. But this year, the box is a little bit different from last year. The toy inside is a little bit changed, so when you try to guess using last year’s clues, they don’t work as well.

This is a bit like the flu vaccine. Every year, doctors try to guess which flu “bug” (a tiny germ) will come to visit. They make a special medicine (the vaccine) to help our bodies get ready and fight it off.

But sometimes, the flu bug changes a little bit before it comes. So, this year’s vaccine is not as good at helping our bodies recognize and fight that new, slightly changed flu bug. That’s why some people say “this year’s flu vaccine is not so good”—because the guess wasn’t quite right.

But don’t worry! The vaccine still helps some people, and doctors keep trying to make better guesses every year.
